title: 3 Big Mistakes Teachers Make When Enforcing Consequences ing-consequences/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Building on prior advice about consistency, Linsin identifies three specific mistakes that undermine consequences even when a teacher is otherwise consistent. The first is showing displeasure through sighs, glares, or frowns, which turns enforcement into a personal feud rather than an impersonal application of rules, causing students to seethe rather than reflect. The second is waiting for a verbal response or asking why a student misbehaved, which invites arguing, justification, or denial rather than reflection, and wastes valuable time. The third is adding personal commentary while escorting a student to time-out or checking on them there, which interferes with the student reaching their own conclusions — a process he considers central to time-out's value. His recommended alternative is a short, scripted, unemotional delivery: state the rule broken, apply the consequence, and walk away, letting the plan do its job without further engagement.
points: Showing visible displeasure when enforcing consequences turns discipline into a personal feud rather than impersonal accountability.
Waiting for a student's verbal response or asking why they misbehaved invites arguing and wastes time.
Adding personal commentary while escorting a student to time-out interferes with their own process of reflection.
The correct approach is a short, unemotional, scripted delivery: state the rule broken, apply the consequence, and walk away.
Enforcing consequences this way protects the teacher-student relationship and empowers students to learn from their mistakes.
quotes: Sighing, glaring, frowning, and the like create friction and animosity, which takes the focus off the student and their misbehavior and makes it a personal feud between you.
Another common mistake is to enforce a consequence and then wait for a response. Most teachers do this because they want the student to verbally answer for their misbehavior.
It provides an opening for the student to justify for their misbehavior, point the finger elsewhere, or try to convince you that you didn’t see what you just saw.

Instead of allowing the consequence to work, the teacher will express their disappointment in the student. They’ll tell them how they should feel, what they should think, and how they should behave the next time.
When a student misbehaves, your only job is to inform. It’s to hold accountable in the least disruptive way so your classroom management plan can do its good work.
This way, you safeguard your relationship with the student. You allow them to ponder their mistake and take responsibility for it.
